rewrites.summary:
France is very safe for a transgender visitor, with risk concentrated on two specific situations. If you are arrested for any reason, including a protest or minor offence, a trans woman is likely to be placed in a men's prison on the basis of her legal gender — a systemic practice documented with foreign trans women (Argentine, Ecuadorian) subjected to genital-exam "verification," isolation and abuse, and confirmed in a 2025 case in which a trans detainee was held in a men's prison in isolation; France's own detention watchdog says trans detainees "suffer the most."

At the border, trans women — especially racialised or Latin-American travellers — have been humiliated by border police (the documented Giovanna case at a main international airport), and airport waiting-zones draw repeated discrimination criticism.

Offsetting this: there is no restriction on bathroom use, and the social norm leans trans-inclusive (a Lyon hostel in 2024 sanctioned a guest who complained about a trans person in a female dorm as "transphobic"). Anti-discrimination and hate-crime law cover gender identity, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013, so partner travel raises no recognition gap. The risk is harassment-level in day-to-day tourism, with the serious-but-rare arrest/placement axis being the main caveat.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The placement issue stays politically live: the custodial-inspection authority's 2021 opinion (building on one from 2010) found serious, persistent violations and no marked improvement despite the 2016 gender-recognition reform, and a 2025 parliamentary question on the case of a trans detainee held in a men's prison drew official scrutiny of the prison system's inability to guarantee conditions for trans detainees.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing data shows persistent discrimination: the national rights ombudsman's framework decision confirms fundamental-rights violations from case files and association testimony, citing the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Urban crime (pickpocketing, theft) in Paris and Marseille, and the general risk of civil unrest/protests, affect all travellers.

The cited placement and border-policing evidence centres on trans women, and the border-friction account dates from 2017; no cited source covers trans male visitors' detention experience.

blindSourceSummaries: Placement of trans women in prisons follows the gender inscribed on identity documents, creating a legal grey area — facilities improvise with special units or isolation, restricting contact with other inmates; accounts describe assault vulnerability and suicide risk. No statutory rule governs placement, so treatment varies by facility.

The national custodial-inspection authority's opinion of 25 May 2021, reviewing roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 plus ministry and association input, finds serious, persistent violations — placement by birth sex, isolation, strip-search exposure — and notes no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the nation's 2016 legal gender-recognition reform; it issues binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

An interview with the national preventive mechanism explains why a new opinion was issued — the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, gender-recognition law and terminology changed, and the new opinion extends coverage to intersex and non-binary detainees; it cites structural problems (isolation of vulnerable people, suicide prevention) built on a decade of letters from detained trans people.

A trans woman detained in connection with a motorway protest has been held since late 2024 in a men's prison and kept in isolation — confirming that as of 2025 trans detainees are still placed in facilities matching birth sex, with isolation used as the management response.

A deputy formally questions the top government lawyer on a trans inmate's incarceration, arguing the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees — official parliamentary scrutiny keeping the placement issue politically live.

A first-person account describes routine humiliation by border police at an airport, with the traveller publicly questioned in front of other travellers — visitor-facing evidence of identity-document friction at entry points.

A report describes a hostel incident in which a guest who objected to a man in a female dormitory bathroom was threatened with 'transphobia' by the manager — a traveller-facing dispute over sex-segregated accommodation, contested framing notwithstanding.

The national rights ombudsman's framework decision on trans rights confirms persistent fundamental-rights violations from case files and association testimony, and cites a rights agency's 2023 survey — 64% of trans people report identity-related discrimination — with official guidance for service providers.

A report on the nation's first same-sex wedding, performed days after the marriage-equality law took effect — dating the legal equality baseline relevant to partner travel and marriage recognition for visitors.

rewrites.summary:
Poland is broadly workable with two genuinely traveler-relevant weaknesses. In detention, documented severe failures involve foreign trans people directly: a Vietnamese trans woman was held in a male immigration-detention center with her hormone-therapy needs ignored for three months, until the border authorities ordered her release after intervention, and the European Court of Human Rights found in 2024 that the country violated a trans prisoner's rights by denying her hormone therapy. There is no specialized trans prison section.

Socially, the climate was deeply hostile under the previous government ("LGBT-free zones") and is improving under the current coalition — a hate-speech reform draft appeared in March 2025, and in June 2024 the directive blocking recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad was revoked — but a low baseline persists: Pride marches have been violently attacked (Białystok 2019), online anti-LGBT harassment is documented (Amnesty 2025), and rural areas draw harassment warnings.

Bathrooms are unrestricted and there is no cross-dressing statute. Gender-marker documents run through the civil-status-records regime, whose sufficiency a 2024 scholarly analysis questions. A government travel advisory lists sexual orientation among reported harassment motives alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and major cities are calmer than rural areas.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Litigation and legislative flux around the social baseline: the European Court of Human Rights ruled in September 2024 that the lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum and called for a recognition framework; the hate-speech reform draft that emerged in March 2025 passed the national legislation centre in May, but approval was postponed, with a second bill following in late October; a 2007 proposal to punish anyone promoting homosexuality in schools documents the prior hostile posture.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The court-based, medically gatekept LGR regime, with no self-ID, is resident-facing; the ECtHR HRT-denial ruling concerned a resident prisoner.

Resident discrimination data: a report by the rights organisation Amnesty International documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence against the LGBTI community, including the LGBT-free-zones legacy (2019-23) and platform policy reversals (a misgendering/deadnaming rule removed in April 2023 and reinstated in 2024).
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Passport theft, unofficial-taxis overcharging, and general urban crime affect all travellers.

blindSourceSummaries: A regional court placed a transgender woman in a guarded centre for male foreigners; after intervention, the border authorities ordered her release. Her hormone therapy had been interrupted for three months because the centre refused medication supply; the case also documented her prior violence and sexual-assault history.

On 11 July 2024, a human-rights court found prison authorities violated a convention article (and rejected another) by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy; damages of EUR 8,000 were ordered. Precedent: trans prisoners can litigate medication denial and win.

A rights organisation's 2025 report documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence against the country's LGBTI community online, including the LGBT-free-zone legacy (2019-23), lack of legal inclusion, and platform policy reversals (a misgendering/deadnaming rule removed April 2023, reinstated 2024).

A world-report chapter on the country (events of 2024) says LGBT-rights reform was slow and insufficient; in June 2024 the directive blocking recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad was revoked, and in September a human-rights court ruled the lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum, calling for a recognition framework.

An annual review chapter (Jan-Dec 2024) reports a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft penal-code amendment raised penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence and passed the government legislation centre in May, but approval was postponed; a second bill followed in late October; the top government lawyer set up a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

A national travel advisory lists sexual orientation among reported harassment motives alongside physical appearance and foreigner status; it links generic LGBTQ2+ travel guidance and notes visa-free stays of up to 90 days for tourists. Generic advisory, limited country-specific finding.

A scholarly legal analysis of the country's administrative regime for transgender persons under the civil-status-records law, population register act and identity-cards act asks whether citizens are equally treated and whether protection is sufficient, especially on civil status — evidence of how gender-marker documents work in practice.

A 2007 news release reports a then-government proposal for fast-track legislation punishing anyone promoting homosexuality in schools — dismissal, fines or prison for teachers and students, banning LGBT organisations and safer-sex HIV education; a rights organisation wrote to the prime minister. Historical precedent for national school censorship.

rewrites.summary:
Hungary is in a fast-improving post-Orbán transition. The most acute traveler-facing risk — the 2025 Pride ban with facial-recognition identification of attendees — has stopped: the 2026 Budapest Pride was held freely after the April 2026 election in which Péter Magyar's Tisza party won a supermajority, ending 16 years of previous rule.

However, the era's laws remain on the books: a total ban on domestic legal gender recognition (2020), the 2021 "child protection" content law, and a constitutional amendment banning LGBTQ public events. The structural weakness that has not changed with the election is detention: a German court in 2025 blocked the extradition of a non-binary person because of prison conditions and the person's identity, and watchdogs report transphobia in prisons with a "culture of silence."

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation of trans identity, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific entry friction. Social hostility lingers outside Budapest, the capital, but the government-led demonization that characterised the previous years has ended.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Judicial flux: the EU's top court has ruled that the 2021 "child protection" law breaches EU values, handing the new government a repeal mandate, and a 2025 judgment obliges the register authority to rectify recorded gender data where it has changed and no longer complies with accuracy principles.

Legislative trajectory for events: a March 2025 law banned organising or participating in Pride, and the 2025 permit denial followed in June — the last pre-election restrictions before the 2026 Pride was held freely; the 2020 rollback made legal gender recognition explicitly illegal from that year.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The 2020 total ban on domestic legal gender recognition is resident-facing; it redefined 'nem' as immutable biological sex, forcing trans residents to carry mismatched documents (a de facto impossibility since 2018, explicitly illegal since 2020).

The prison "culture of silence" affects resident detainees; a 2025 national report on LGBTIQ detainees documents the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in detention amid the current legal and political climate.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.

As of the September 2026 freshness check, the 2020 gender-recognition ban and the 2021 child-protection law remain in force; repeal depends on the new supermajority, and the pace of change is unverified.

rewrites.summary:
Czechia is broadly workable with an improving trajectory and a major welcoming tourist hub (Prague), offset by unprepared detention systems and elevated baseline social hostility. If detained, the system is unprepared: a documented case shows police mishandling the extradition-detention of an HIV-positive trans foreigner; safeguards ordered at the highest court level exist, but practice is inconsistent.

About half of LGBTIQ people report being targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years, and a far-right party uses "deviant" rhetoric; Prague and larger cities are welcoming, but harassment is more likely in rural areas or late at night.

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation of trans identity, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation flux: the Constitutional Court struck the surgery requirement in April 2024, the European Court of Human Rights found in September 2025 that the surgical and sterilisation conditions for official sex change violated private-life rights, and a criminal-code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity awaits parliament.

Political and legislative context: after the LGR ruling a minister publicly stated the goal of "preventing men from giving birth," far-right election leaflets promised to take money from "LGBT activists," and a marriage-equality bill has cleared committees since 2023.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The LGR reform (medical diagnosis plus 6–12 months' observation, no surgery) is a resident-facing process; the Supreme Court's November 2025 demand for prison rules concerns resident detainees.

Resident discrimination data: 43% of LGBTIQ people report discrimination or harassment over five years, with the highest share among trans and non-binary respondents; 51% report insults, assault or threats, and police recorded 94 hate crimes in 2024, with 46 prosecuted and 42 sentenced.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Pickpocketing and fake-plainclothes-police scams in Prague, the capital, affect all tourists.

blindSourceSummaries: A top court's official legal summary (April 2024) struck down the requirement that surgery including sterilisation be a condition for official legal sex change, holding a sex change conditional on disabling reproductive function unconstitutional — the landmark end of compulsory sterilisation for legal gender recognition.
Note: not retrievable at research time; the underlying report (June 2025) covers the country dropping the surgery requirement for legal gender change.

Administrative courts clashed over immigration-police handling of a detained trans foreigner — the highest administrative court rebuked a lower court for moralising and ruled authorities must first assess whether detainees are 'potentially vulnerable persons' before placement: detention-placement safeguards exist at the highest court level but practice is inconsistent.

Prisons are unprepared for trans people and lack clear rules; the highest court demands the national prison concept explicitly address the needs of people in or after transition, citing the ruling that no longer conditions legal gender change on surgery; the human-rights commissioner pushes a binding regulation while the justice ministry claims the existing framework suffices (consultation ongoing).

An annual review (covering 2023) reports survey findings — 43% discriminated or harassed in the past five years, highest among trans and non-binary respondents; 51% targeted by insults, assault or threats in five years; politicians' anti-LGBT speech rose from 43% (2018) to 71% (2023); a group disrupted a Pride drag story-time with homophobic slurs; a new asylum law includes SOGI grounds; a marriage-equality bill cleared committees in June while a constitutional ban moved to second reading; a regional court ordered re-issued certificates and a diploma for a trans graduate; no law yet ending mandatory sterilisation as of 2023.

An annual review (covering 2024) reports that after the court repealed the surgical prerequisite, a minister publicly stated his goal was 'to prevent men from giving birth' and other politicians issued transphobic statements; far-right leaflets promised to take money from 'LGBT activists'; the government approved a criminal-code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity (pending in parliament), while a court ruling weakened 'particularly vulnerable victim' status; school-curriculum LGBTI content prompted organised parental opt-out campaigns.
thin: no usable finding

A travel portal (Feb 2026) rates two major cities as the most open for LGBTQ+ solo travellers — formal nondiscrimination policies, queer districts, hostels with concierge support, private rooms and organised socials; harassment risk concentrates in rural areas and late-night settings; practical guidance on documents, medication carriage and venues.

A 2024 hate-crime report: police recorded 94 hate crimes in 2024, 46 prosecuted, 42 sentenced (LGBTI-motivated incidents included in the bias breakdown); criminal-code amendments abandon the 'hostility model' for the discriminatory-selection model; a key observation — recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes.

A judgment (12 Sep 2025) found a violation of private-life rights regarding legal-gender-recognition conditions — the surgical/sterilisation condition for official sex change and related civil-registry treatment held incompatible with private-life rights; the court's reasoning frames gender recognition through self-determination.

A news report (2018) on a caretaker government backing a same-sex marriage bill introduced by a cross-party group of deputies to replace registered partnerships — an early marker of the marriage-equality legislative trail still running.

rewrites.summary:
Serbia is a dangerous destination for trans visitors despite no criminalisation. The most acute documented traveler-axis risk is police: in February 2024 the interior ministry began investigating officers who beat, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during a Belgrade apartment raid. About 105 sexual-orientation/gender-identity-motivated incidents were recorded in 2024, and Pride marches require heavy police protection.

The country is outside the Schengen border-free travel area, so border checks apply to foreign travellers.

The bottom line for visitors: police-brutality risk and weak protection make it a high-risk destination despite no criminalisation, with the major-tourist city "conditionally" manageable under situational awareness.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Political context: the country's lesbian prime minister is symbolically visible, but stalled legislation and police brutality make that largely symbolic rather than substantive protection.

Enforcement context: the 2024 police-violence probe had not produced a public outcome at reporting time, and the Pride information centre announced closure after repeated attacks with none properly sanctioned.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The stalled Law on Gender Identity and the weakly enforced anti-discrimination law are resident-facing; the Belgrade prison's trans-sensitive search policy concerns resident detainees; the documented testosterone supply-chain disruptions affect residents on HRT.

Resident discrimination data: a standing civil-society register tallied about 105 bias-motivated incidents in 2024, an analysis counted 70 instances of politicians' hate speech (April 2023 to April 2024), and a survey found three-quarters of trans and non-binary people fear job interviews due to anticipated discrimination.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: General crime and border-corruption affect all travellers; the country is not inside the Schengen border-free travel area, so border checks apply to foreigners.

rewrites.summary:
Croatia is broadly workable with a cleaner documented traveler-axis profile than its regional neighbours: no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality case, or foreign-trans-detention case surfaced in the research. The Dalmatian coast's international-tourism culture (Dubrovnik, Hvar, Split) is broadly open, and Zagreb, the capital, has the region's most established gay scene.

The framework is weaker than many peer nations': legal gender recognition (available since 2015) is partial and not self-ID, covering only some documents; there is no marriage equality (a 2013 constitutional ban), and an anti-gender movement is active. A 2024 prosecution of a host who refused to accommodate a gay couple shows enforcement works.

The Catholic-conservative climate is more marked outside the main tourist areas. The country, an EU and Schengen member, sits inside the border-free travel area, so border friction for most travellers is low.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is broadly workable with a cleaner documented traveler-axis profile than its regional neighbours: no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality case, or foreign-trans-detention case surfaced in the research. The coast's international-tourism culture is broadly open, and the capital has the region's most established gay scene.

The framework is weaker than many peer nations': legal gender recognition (available since 2015) is partial and not self-ID, covering only some documents; there is no marriage equality (a 2013 constitutional ban), and an anti-gender movement is active. A 2024 prosecution of a host who refused to accommodate a gay couple shows enforcement works.

The Catholic-conservative climate is more marked outside the main tourist areas. The country sits inside the border-free travel area, so border friction for most travellers is low.

blindSourceSummaries: A documentation report on implementation of a council recommendation covers hate-crime legislation and under-reporting of homophobic and transphobic crimes, hate-speech case studies, freedom of assembly, legal gender recognition, same-sex partnership recognition, employment discrimination, and compiled hate-crime data with case studies.

An annual review chapter reports a prosecutor charged a man for refusing a gay couple's accommodation booking (2018 incident); anti-gender disinformation escalating — a parliamentary session on 'Gender Ideology' featured speakers spreading misinformation and no LGBTI organisations invited; a first Pride march in a coastal city faced disruption the day before.

A legal journal article analyses how police, customs and court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming persons under national law — built on the 2013 legislative amendment allowing gender-marker registration without altering sex characteristics, working through the criminal procedure act, police powers act, customs act and prison-sentences law with case studies of search difficulties.

An official human-rights report on the country says minority representatives report that anti-discrimination provisions (employment, housing, education, health) are not consistently enforced; NGOs report the judiciary's uneven handling of discrimination cases and limited justice access, with victims reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and victimisation during trial; hate-crime investigations flagged as inadequate.

A country overview: same-sex conduct legal since 1977; life partnerships since 2014 while a 2013 constitutional referendum banned same-sex marriage; full same-sex adoption rights since 2022; open military service; hate-crime legislation; Pride events in multiple cities; legal gender recognition framework — the reference backbone for dated milestones.

A travel guide reports the country widely accepts LGBTQIA+ travellers — but public displays of affection may draw unwelcome responses in less populated cities and gay venues are virtually non-existent outside the capital, now improving with new venues in coastal and interior towns.

A legal experts' country report on non-discrimination (2024, reporting period 2023) covers transposition and implementation of the region's equality directives, including sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds.

A local news report documents a city getting an LGBT centre (the second in the country, first on the coast) before the city's Pride; organisers demanded equal treatment of same-sex families (marriage, joint adoption) and said institutions create 'second-class citizens'; the mayor attended the press conference.

A local news report covers the presentation of an LGBTIQ+ centre in a second major city — founded to develop the community in the surrounding county and network with national and international organisations, backed publicly by the mayor and cultural institutions; goals include visibility, anti-discrimination work and quality-of-life advocacy.

rewrites.summary:
The country is broadly workable, at the lower end, with one of Europe's most restrictive legal-gender-recognition situations. Lithuania's Civil Code grants the right to medically change gender in principle, but no legal framework regulating the procedure has existed for 17 years — a deadlock the Constitutional Court refused to resolve in September 2025, perpetuating what an ECtHR body called a "distressing legal uncertainty."

Socially, a conservative climate is well documented: an MP called LGBT people "degenerated" and "spreading diseases" (his immunity was revoked), "traditional family values" groups disrupt peaceful protests, and an ombudsperson found police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to assembly. Trans people report systemic workplace harassment — open ridicule, isolation, and psychological abuse.

There is no criminalisation, and the national Pride in 2024 drew a large crowd of 15,000.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation flux: after a regional district court suspended a civil case on amending civil-status gender documents and referred the laws' constitutionality, the Constitutional Court declined in September 2025 to examine the absence of provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes.

Historical legislation: five anti-gay and anti-trans bills were considered in 2013, including a ban on gender reassignment and fines for organisers of events "denigrating constitutional moral values"; a 2009 minors law banning information on homosexuality in schools and media accessible to minors was passed over a presidential veto — the historical baseline of the current climate.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The 17-year legal-gender-recognition deadlock is resident-facing: the Civil Code grants the right to medically change gender in principle, but implementing legislation has never been adopted, leaving trans people in legal limbo.

The workplace-harassment documentation (open ridicule, isolation, psychological abuse) is resident-facing and systemic; the "Protection of Minors" dissemination law is a resident/climate signal, weakened in its same-sex-family provision by a 2024 ruling.

Resident-facing context: the national ombudsperson's 2024 review covers public attitudes, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination and data protection; LGBTI asylum seekers were granted protection after a four-year wait, with dire camp conditions and a psychologist convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

blindSourceSummaries: The top court refused to address the country's trans rights gap — a significant setback; the civil code grants unmarried adults the right to medically change gender, but implementing legislation has never been adopted, leaving trans people in legal limbo.

A regional district court suspended a civil case on amending civil-status gender documents and referred the laws' compliance with the constitution to the top court — asking whether courts could finally end 17 years of legal limbo.

The top court declined to examine a lower court's request to review the absence of legal provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents.
Trans people in the country detail workplace harassment — open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse; systemic labour-market discrimination per experts.

The parliament's ombudsperson found police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly — inadequate police response to hostile provocateurs; recommended measures to guarantee effective assembly rights.

The equal-opportunities ombudsperson's summary of the 2024 national review on the situation of transgender people covers public attitudes, the legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and negative public attitudes; it notes the lack of a legal framework and strategic approach.

An annual review chapter reports a systemic lack of targeted hate-crime victim support; LGBTI asylum seekers granted protection after a four-year wait, with dire camp conditions and a psychologist convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts; prosecution of a former MP for anti-LGBTI ridicule was complicated by his elected-official immunity.

A report on parliament considering five anti-gay and anti-trans bills — including a ban on gender reassignment, a same-sex adoption ban, fines for organisers of events 'denigrating constitutional moral values', and legalisation of anti-gay speech.

A report that parliament passed a law banning information on homosexuality in schools and media accessible to minors, overriding a presidential veto; a rights organisation called it a huge step backwards.

rewrites.summary:
Latvia is broadly workable with no legal framework for gender recognition — trans people cannot legally change their gender marker, leaving those who have transitioned in a legal limbo. The most documented institutional failure is the European Court of Human Rights' ruling in Hanovs v. Latvia (2024), which found the country failed to prosecute a homophobic hate crime, violating the prohibition of inhuman treatment and the right to private life.

On the positive side, an administrative court overturned the denial of asylum to an LGBTI asylum-seeker in 2025, showing some institutional capacity for protection.

There is no criminalisation, and bathrooms are unrestricted.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Neighbour comparison: the documented hostility is less extreme than in the neighbouring country to the south — no "degenerate"-rhetoric MP, no propaganda-style minors law, and no systemic-trans-workplace-harassment study surfaced — which places the country marginally above it.

Litigation flux: the top prosecutor reopened criminal proceedings after the 2024 ruling, and a homophobic attack case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences; a 2007 statement by a senior cleric calling homosexuality "total corruption" and demanding a referendum on same-sex marriage marks the older baseline.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The absence of any legal-gender-recognition framework is resident-facing — trans people cannot legally change their gender marker, leaving those who have transitioned in a legal limbo; the Hanovs hate-crime case and the asylum ruling concern residents.

Resident and social data: civil unions for same-sex couples have been in force since 1 July 2024, while transgender and non-binary people still lack targeted legal change; a trans immigrant reports that legal transition would invalidate his marriage and residency status; two people were attacked in a regional city, with the investigation reopened after police closed it.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

A human-rights-court press release (18 July 2024) reports the Court unanimously found violations of three articles after a homophobic attack — no criminal charges were brought despite the aggressor admitting anti-gay slurs; the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences.

An annual review chapter reports an administrative court overturned denial of asylum to an LGBTI seeker; the top prosecutor reopened criminal proceedings in the hate-crime case after the court ruling; two people were attacked in a regional city, with the top prosecutor ordering the investigation reopened after police closed it; a former MEP's homophobic posts were investigated.

An analysis of the ruling clarifies the positive obligations of nations in homophobic-attack cases — thorough investigation and punishment of hate crimes, sending a message of zero tolerance; it notes the troubling pattern of regional nations failing to protect LGBTI+ persons and to investigate effectively.

An organisation's country page records the human-rights-court judgment — violations of three articles after authorities declined to prosecute a homophobic assault on a gay couple as a hate-motivated offence.

A 2007 report quotes a senior cleric calling homosexuality 'total corruption in the sexual arena' and 'an unnatural form of prostitution', demanding a referendum on same-sex marriage and counter-Pride crowds of tens of thousands, calling Pride a 'foreign-inspired action'.
A 2018 report: several thousand people marched in a regional Pride in the capital — the annual event rotating among regional capitals, organised by a local association.
